abstract: Classical models of embryonic patterning explain how cells acquire positional identities by responding to different concentration thresholds along morphogen gradients. Yet many developmental systems generate spatial patterns through temporal programs of gene expression, raising the question of how these programs translate into spatial organization. In the short-germ insect Tribolium castaneum, for example, periodic pair-rule gene expression that drives segmentation and nonperiodic gap-gene expression that specifies regional identities emerge sequentially at the posterior and propagate anteriorly as waves. To investigate how these temporal programs give rise to spatial patterns, we developed a sequential multiplexed imaging strategy based on hybridization chain reaction (HCR), allowing us to visualize up to ten anterior-posterior (AP) patterning genes within the same embryo. We combined this approach with intronic-exonic labeling to infer gene-expression dynamics and characterize the propagation of expression domains. Our analysis revealed that gap-gene expression domains remain dynamic and continue to propagate during tissue elongation. To test whether spatial organization preserves the temporal sequence established at the posterior, we compared the temporal order of expression peaks and half-height borders with their relative spatial positions along the AP axis. Primary pair-rule genes generally preserved the expected order, whereas some gap-gene landmarks appeared in a different relative order in space than in time. Together with the continued propagation of gap-gene domains, these findings suggest that their spatial organization does not simply preserve the initial temporal sequence but can change as expression propagates anteriorly. Such differences could arise because gene-expression domains propagate at different speeds, because regulatory interactions between genes change as expression propagates away from the posterior, or both. Our findings therefore suggest that translating time into space involves more than preserving a temporal sequence: the process can also reshape the relationships among gene-expression domains as spatial patterns emerge.
